question: On 22 May 2026, the International Monetary Fund reportedly urged Spain to phase out broad fuel and energy support measures and to harmonise VAT rates, while recommending targeted protection for vulnerable households. Spain had adopted temporary fuel-tax relief after March 2026 energy price tensions, including a VAT cut on fuels from 21 % to 10 % and a reduction of hydrocarbon duties to EU minimum levels.

In normal conditions, taxes accounted for around 50 % of the final petrol price and 43 % of diesel in Spain in 2025. Such measures are socially regressive when millions of workers, self-employed people, rural families and lower-income households have no real alternative to private transport.

Removing fuel relief is not a neutral fiscal adjustment; it is an immediate increase in the cost of working, transporting goods and accessing basic services. EU economic governance must not become an instrument for pushing Member States into fiscal harmonisation or indirect tax increases against their citizens. 1.

Does the Commission intend to recommend, request or incentivise Spain, through the European Semester, fiscal surveillance or any EU funding framework, to withdraw fueltax relief or energy-support measures?
Will the Commission rule out linking EU funds, fiscal assessments or country-specific recommendations to VAT harmonisation or higher fuel taxation in Spain?
How will the Commission assess the distributive impact on workers and lower-income households before supporting such measures?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) 1.

In the Recommendation for a Council Recommendation of 3 June 20261, the Commission recommended that Spain act in 2026 and 2027 to ensure that measures addressing higher energy prices are temporary, targeted at addressing the needs of vulnerable households or energy-intensive firms, preserve incentives for energy savings, and remain consistent with the EU fiscal framework. 2.

Under Spain’s Recovery and Resilience Plan, agreed measures for tax reform included the entry into force of reforms based on the Committee of Experts’ recommendations or other Ministry of Finance analyses in areas including environmental, corporate, wealth and health taxation, personal income tax on capital income, as well as diesel tax increases.
Additionally, where relevant, the European Semester incorporates country-specific policy recommendations on the quality and composition of Member States’ tax systems. 3.

With its Affordable Energy Action Plan2 and its AccelerateEU Communication3, the Commission has implemented and assisted Member States in implementing short- and longterm measures to ensure affordable energy and protect consumers from the impacts of the energy crisis, particularly vulnerable households and the most affected sectors.

Generally, value-added tax (VAT) rates reduction cannot be targeted to specific users, which makes VAT less efficient in targeting vulnerable consumers. At the same time, Member States have the possibility to, for example, reduce VAT rates as low as 5% to promote electrification. The Commission has assessed the distributional impact of higher fuel prices on households across income groups4.
